faq.question: How to get my diplomas recognized?
faq.answer: Contact the qualifications recognition body of the target country (e.g. ENIC-NARIC in Europe). The procedure usually takes 2-3 months.

faq.question: Do I need a work permit?
faq.answer: It depends on your nationality and destination country. EU/EEA citizens generally don't need a permit to work in the EU.

faq.question: What budget to plan for housing?
faq.answer: Plan 30-40% of your income for rent. Add 2-3 months of rent for initial deposit and agency fees.

faq.answer: Offer a guarantor, pay several months in advance, or use services like Garantme to reassure landlords.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Everything you need to know before starting your expatriation.

1.question: Is SkyWalk free?
1.answer: Yes, registration and access to the main features are completely free. We offer comparison tools, a community forum and country guides accessible to everyone.

2.question: Which countries are covered by the platform?
2.answer: We currently cover 4 countries: France, Japan, the United States, and Switzerland, with detailed cost-of-living data across multiple cities in each country. New destinations are added regularly.

3.question: How does the cost of living comparator work?
3.answer: Our comparator uses up-to-date data to compare housing, food, transportation and other category prices between your current city and your destination.

4.question: Does SkyWalk help me find a job?
4.answer: Yes! Our search engine aggregates thousands of international job offers via the Adzuna API. You can filter by country, city, contract type and salary.

5.question: How can I connect with other expats?
5.answer: Our community forum allows you to ask questions, share testimonials and receive advice from expats already settled in your target country.

6.question: What administrative procedures are covered?
6.answer: We provide detailed guides on visas, work permits, health insurance, bank account opening and all the key steps for each country.

france.alertText: Social Security covers 70% of medical costs. A supplementary health plan (~€70/month) covers the remaining costs. Long-term conditions (ALD) are fully covered at 100%.

usa.alertText: No universal coverage. Health insurance is usually tied to employer. Marketplace (ACA): ~$450/month on average. Uninsured care is extremely expensive. Visit healthcare.gov.

japan.alertTitle: National Health Insurance (国民健康保険)
japan.alertText: Health insurance is mandatory in Japan. Residents pay ~30% of care (70% reimbursed). NHI costs about ¥25,000/month. Dental and optical care partially covered.

switzerland.alertText: Basic health insurance (LAMal) is MANDATORY for all residents. Among the highest premiums in Europe (~393 CHF/month). Dental and optical care NOT covered by LAMal.

checklist-avant-depart.title: The complete checklist before your move abroad
checklist-avant-depart.excerpt: From cancelling your contracts to preparing your documents, everything you need to do before expatriating.
checklist-avant-depart.content:
## Why a checklist is essential

Expatriating is a major life project involving dozens of administrative, logistical and personal steps. Without rigorous organization, it's easy to forget a crucial step that could delay your departure or complicate your settlement.

## 6 months before departure

Start with the longest procedures: visa application, diploma recognition, and job search if you don't have one yet. This is also the time to evaluate your budget and start saving to cover the first months.

## 3 months before departure

Notify your employer if you are employed. Start the process of cancelling your contracts (rent, insurance, subscriptions). Make an appointment with your doctor for a health check-up and update your vaccinations.

## 1 month before departure

Finalize your temporary accommodation at your destination. Pack your bags by checking luggage restrictions. Make certified copies of all your important documents. Inform your bank of your departure.

## The week of departure

Check that your passport and visa are in order. Keep essential documents with you: tickets, insurance, accommodation address. Say goodbye to your loved ones and enjoy this moment of transition.

## Essential documents

- Valid passport (check expiration date)
- Visa or residence permit
- Employment or study contract
- International health insurance certificate
- Recent bank statements
- Certified translations of your diplomas
- Apostilled birth certificate
- International driving licence

budget-expatriation.title: How to estimate and manage your expatriation budget
budget-expatriation.excerpt: Hidden costs, expense items to anticipate and tips for managing your finances abroad.
budget-expatriation.content:
## Budget, the cornerstone of your expatriation

The financial aspect is often the primary source of stress for expatriates. Between moving costs, first rents, visa fees and settling in, the bill can quickly add up if not anticipated.

## Pre-departure costs

Before even leaving your country, plan a budget for visa fees (€150-500 depending on the country), certified translations (€30-80 per document), medical check-up (€100-300), and potentially an international move (€2,000-8,000 depending on volume).

## Settlement budget

The first three months are usually the most expensive. You need to account for the housing deposit (1-3 months rent), essential furniture, opening bank accounts, and subscribing to local insurance. Plan a financial cushion of 3 to 6 months of running expenses.

## Managing exchange rates

If you keep income in your original currency, exchange rate fluctuations can significantly impact your purchasing power. Use services like Wise or Revolut to minimize conversion fees.

## Tip: the monthly tracking spreadsheet

Create a simple table with your fixed expense items (rent, insurance, transport) and variable ones (food, leisure, contingencies). Compare each month to identify areas where you can optimize.

demarches-visa.title: Understanding visa procedures in 2026
demarches-visa.excerpt: Visa types, timelines, required documents and mistakes to avoid for each visa category.
demarches-visa.content:
## The visa, your key to expatriation

The visa is the most important administrative document of your expatriation project. Understanding the different types and procedures will save you precious time and avoid rejections.

## Main visa types

There are generally tourist visas (short stay), work visas (sponsored by an employer), student visas, entrepreneur/investor visas, and family reunification. Each category has its own criteria and timelines.

## Expected timelines

Timelines vary considerably depending on the country and visa type. Allow 2-4 weeks for a tourist visa, 2-6 months for a work visa, and up to 12 months for certain investor visas. Always start your procedures as early as possible.

## Most common mistakes

- Incomplete file or untranslated documents
- Photos not conforming to required standards
- Form filled with errors or inconsistencies
- Underestimated processing time
- Passport expiring within less than 6 months

## Tip: the bulletproof file

Prepare an organized file with dividers, copies of each document, and a clear cover letter explaining your project. Consulates appreciate well-structured files, it speeds up processing.

choc-culturel.title: Overcoming culture shock: the 4 phases of adaptation
choc-culturel.excerpt: Understanding the psychological stages of cultural adaptation to better experience your expatriation.
choc-culturel.content:
## Culture shock, a universal reality

Regardless of your level of preparation, culture shock affects all expatriates. Understanding this phenomenon and its phases will help you get through it with serenity.

## Phase 1: The honeymoon

The first weeks are often euphoric. Everything is new, exciting, different. You are fascinated by the local culture, food, landscapes. This phase usually lasts 1 to 3 months.

## Phase 2: Frustration

Daily reality sets in. The cultural differences that amused you become sources of irritation. The language barrier weighs heavily, homesickness sets in. This phase is the most difficult but it is normal and temporary.

## Phase 3: Adjustment

Gradually, you develop coping strategies. You better understand cultural codes, you create routines, you make local friends. Daily life becomes smoother.

## Phase 4: Acceptance

You have found your balance between your culture of origin and your host culture. You no longer seek to compare but to appreciate both. You have become bicultural.

## Tips for getting through culture shock

- Join expat groups to share your experiences
- Learn the local language, even the basics
- Keep in touch with loved ones back home
- Actively explore your new neighbourhood and city
- Be patient and kind to yourself

trouver-emploi-etranger.title: Finding a job abroad: complete guide 2026
trouver-emploi-etranger.excerpt: Search strategies, CV adaptation, platforms to use and sectors recruiting expatriates.
trouver-emploi-etranger.content:
## The international job market in 2026

The international job market has evolved considerably in recent years. Remote work, digital nomad visas and talent shortages in certain sectors are opening new opportunities for expatriates.

## Adapting your CV to local standards

Each country has its own CV conventions. In the United States, no photo or age. In Japan, the Rirekisho format is standard. In Switzerland, a detailed 2-3 page CV is appreciated. Research the standards of your target country.

## Essential platforms

LinkedIn remains the universal platform, but each country has its local champions. Use specialized expat job boards like SkyWalk, and don't hesitate to contact companies directly.

## Sectors that are hiring

IT and digital, healthcare, engineering, language teaching and hospitality are sectors where international demand remains strong in 2026.

## Networking, your best asset

Over 70% of international positions are filled through networking. Attend professional events, join expat associations, and activate your existing network.

logement-premier-mois.title: Finding housing for your first months of expatriation
logement-premier-mois.excerpt: Temporary solutions, pitfalls to avoid and tips for securing accommodation remotely.
logement-premier-mois.content:
## Don't rush

The biggest mistake is wanting to sign a long-term lease before arriving. Opt for a temporary solution (Airbnb, flatshare, furnished residence) for your first 1-3 months. This gives you time to discover neighbourhoods and search calmly.

## Temporary solutions

Platforms like Airbnb, Spotahome or HousingAnywhere offer furnished accommodation for medium durations. Student residences or international flatshares are also excellent options to start with.

## Watch out for scams

Never send money before visiting a property (in person or by video). Beware of offers that seem too good, landlords who won't show the property, and requests for international wire transfers.

## Commonly requested documents

- ID or passport
- Employment contract or proof of income
- Local guarantor (sometimes required for foreigners)
- Bank statements for the last 3 months
- Home insurance certificate

assurance-sante-expatrie.title: Health insurance abroad: the essential guide
assurance-sante-expatrie.excerpt: CFE, international private insurance or local system: how to choose the right coverage for your situation.
assurance-sante-expatrie.content:
## Health, an absolute priority

Health coverage is a crucial issue for every expatriate. An accident or illness abroad without adequate insurance can have devastating financial consequences.

## The three main options

The CFE (Caisse des Français de l'Étranger) offers coverage similar to French Social Security. International private insurance (Allianz, AXA, Cigna) offers more comprehensive but more expensive plans. The local health system is often mandatory and may be sufficient in some countries.

## Choosing the right coverage

Assess your needs: do you have ongoing treatments? Medical history? Do you practice a risky sport? Is your family accompanying you? These criteria determine the level of coverage needed.

## Pitfalls to avoid

- Unanticipated waiting periods
- Exclusions on pre-existing conditions
- Reimbursement caps too low
- Repatriation not included
- Geographic area not covered

## Practical tip

Take out your insurance BEFORE your departure. Always carry your insurance card and emergency numbers. Keep all medical expense receipts to facilitate reimbursements.

temoignage-suisse.title: Testimonial: my expatriation in Switzerland after 2 years
temoignage-suisse.excerpt: Feedback on daily life, cost of living and integration in French-speaking Switzerland.
temoignage-suisse.content:
## Why Switzerland?

I moved to Switzerland two years ago for an engineering position in Geneva. The quality of life, attractive salaries and proximity to France were my main motivations.

## The settlement: more complex than expected

The B permit (foreign worker) was obtained fairly easily thanks to my employer. However, finding accommodation in Geneva was a real obstacle course. Prices are very high and demand far exceeds supply. I ended up settling in Annemasse, on the French side, for my first months.

## The cost of living: the shock

Even with a Swiss salary, the cost of living is surprising. A coffee at 5 CHF, a restaurant meal at 35-50 CHF, health insurance (LAMal) at 430 CHF per month. You have to completely recalibrate your price perception.

## Social integration

The Swiss are welcoming but relationships build slowly. Sports clubs and associations are the best places to create bonds. The French-speaking expat community is also very active and supportive.

## My assessment after 2 years

I don't regret my choice. The quality of life is exceptional, public transport is perfect, nature is everywhere. The salary more than compensates for the cost of living if you manage your budget well.

banque-etranger.title: Opening a bank account abroad: how-to guide
banque-etranger.excerpt: Procedures, required documents and digital alternatives for managing your finances as an expat.
banque-etranger.content:
## Why a local account is essential

A local bank account is essential for receiving your salary, paying your rent and managing your daily expenses. In some countries, it's even a requirement for obtaining a residence permit.

## Generally required documents

- Passport or ID
- Local proof of address
- Visa or residence permit
- Employment contract
- Local tax number (if applicable)

## Digital alternatives

While waiting for your local account, services like Wise, Revolut or N26 allow you to have a European IBAN and make international transfers at low cost. These solutions are also ideal for managing multiple currencies.

## Keep your home country account

It's recommended to keep an account in your home country for recurring debits (taxes, insurance, subscriptions) and as a backup solution in case of problems with your local account.

apprendre-langue.title: Learning the local language: methods and resources
apprendre-langue.excerpt: Apps, immersion courses and daily tips to progress quickly in a new language.
apprendre-langue.content:
## Language, the key to integration

Speaking the local language radically transforms your expatriation experience. Beyond daily communication, it's a sign of respect towards your host country and an integration accelerator.

## Before departure: the basics

Start learning the basics 3-6 months before your departure. Apps like Duolingo, Babbel or Busuu are excellent starting points. Aim for A2 level (basic communication) before arrival.

## On site: immersion

Immersion is the most effective way to progress. Sign up for local courses, find a language tandem, watch local TV, read newspapers. Every interaction is a learning opportunity.

## Free resources

- Podcasts in the target language
- Dedicated YouTube channels
- Tandem apps (HelloTalk, Tandem)
- Municipal libraries (free courses)
- Conversation groups in cafés

## Tip: the vocabulary notebook

Write down 5 new words or expressions heard in your daily life every day. Re-read them in the evening. In one month, you'll have 150 additional words in your active vocabulary.

enfants-expatriation.title: Expatriation with children: how to prepare the move
enfants-expatriation.excerpt: Schooling, psychological adaptation and practical tips for a smooth family expatriation.
enfants-expatriation.content:
## Family expatriation, a shared challenge

Expatriating with children adds an extra dimension to the project. Schooling choices, psychological adaptation and daily management require specific preparation.

## Choosing a school

Three main options are available: local school (total immersion), international school (international curriculum, often in English), and French lycée abroad (continuity of the French system). Each option has advantages depending on the children's age and the planned duration of expatriation.

## Preparing children for departure

Involve your children in the project as early as possible. Show them photos and videos of the country, learn some words of the local language together, read books about the country's culture. The more they feel like active participants in the change, the better they'll accept it.

## Adaptation on site

Children generally adapt faster than adults, especially younger ones. Maintain family rituals that remind them of home (typical meals, video calls with grandparents) while encouraging new friendships and local activities.

## Signs to watch for

- Withdrawal or unusual aggression
- Sudden academic difficulties
- Sleep or eating disorders
- Refusal to go out or participate in activities

If these signs persist beyond a few weeks, don't hesitate to consult a psychologist specializing in international mobility.

temoignage-japon.title: Testimonial: living and working in Japan
temoignage-japon.excerpt: Corporate culture, daily life and surprises: story of an expatriation in the land of the rising sun.
temoignage-japon.content:
## Japan, a dream come true

I had dreamed of Japan since my teenage years. When a professional opportunity presented itself in Tokyo, I didn't hesitate. Here's my feedback after 18 months there.

## Japanese corporate culture

Respect for hierarchy, absolute punctuality and teamwork are the pillars of Japanese professional culture. Meetings are numerous and consensus is sought before any decision. You need to adapt to a different rhythm but it's very enriching.

## Daily life

Tokyo is an incredibly organized and safe city. Public transport is exemplarily punctual, food is excellent and affordable (a bento for 500-800¥), and conveniences are everywhere. The only major challenge: apartment sizes. My 25m² studio costs ¥130,000 per month.

## The language barrier

Contrary to what you might think, English is not widely spoken in everyday Japan. Learning hiragana and katakana is essential for daily life. Kanji will come gradually. Japanese people greatly appreciate efforts to speak their language.

## Daily surprises

- Konbini (24/7 convenience stores) quickly become indispensable
- Waste sorting is an art in itself
- Onsen (hot springs) are an absolute delight
- Politeness is ubiquitous and contagious
- Local festivals (matsuri) are magical moments
